title: SlAIdy

slides.title: SlAIdy
slides.body:
![[fig-slaidy-hero|100%]]

<!-- col -->

**Slides your agent understands.** A deck is markdown and SVG in one HTML file, so an AI agent
reads every slide, writes it and checks its own work.

This deck is the manual: **every slide does what it describes.** Press → to move on, `?` for every key.

#### What this one slide is made of

| | |
|---|---|
| an animated figure | SVG and CSS, 16 kB |
| a formula | $r_{ui} = \mathbf{p}_u^\top \mathbf{q}_i$ |
| a table | this one |
| a link | [github.com/kordikp/slaidy](https://github.com/kordikp/slaidy) |
slides.notes: Ten seconds, one beam. The card starts as what your agent reads: the markdown of a slide and the SVG of its chart. The beam crosses it and leaves the slide behind, each thing where its source was: the heading turns into the title, the rect lines into bars. Then it goes back, because both are the same file. All CSS keyframes; with the animation off, in a print or for a reader who asked for less motion, the figure stops at the split: the slide on the left, its source on the right.
slides.summary: What the project is, shown rather than told: everything the format can carry, on one slide.

slides.title: How to read this deck
slides.body:
![[fig-keys|90%]]

> Press **Esc** and this page is the editor: click any title and type. On a phone, tap to go on.
slides.notes: Everything on the next slides works in the page you are reading: there is no separate viewer, and what you change stays in your browser.
slides.summary: The keys, so the reader can drive the rest of the deck alone.

slides.title: A slide is a few lines of markdown
slides.body:
```markdown
  # Write
  
  ### A few lines of markdown
  *Summary:* what it is for
  *Layout:* two
  
  Words in the left column.
  <!-- col -->
  ![[fig-keys]]
  
  > The line that has to land.
  
  *Delivery note:* what you say.
```

<!-- col -->

A file is a section and `###` starts a slide. The summary says what the slide is for, and the AI
writes to it; a figure is placed by its name.

Export gives back the same files, so **git diffs a talk**, `grep` searches it, and a model reads
every part of it.

> Nothing the app writes is something only the app can read.
slides.summary: The format, shown on a slide like this one.

slides.title: Formulas, tables and code
slides.body:
Write TeX between dollars and the browser draws it, with no library:

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Inline too: user $u$ and item $i$ score $\hat{r}_{ui}=\mathbf{p}_u^\top\mathbf{q}_i$.

<!-- col -->

| A deck of 237 slides | |
|---|---:|
| everything, figures in | 1.0 MB |
| the median figure | 3.7 kB |
| the editor itself | 391 kB |
| dependencies | 0 |

```bash
python3 scripts/build_bundle.py \
  --src slides --figs figures --out talk.json
```
slides.summary: What a technical talk needs, all of it written as text.

slides.title: Click by click
slides.body:
Press → and this slide builds up.

<!-- step -->

- A marker on a line of its own holds what follows for the next click, as `\pause` does in Beamer.

<!-- step -->

- A figure's shapes carry the click they arrive on and the one they leave at, so a drawing builds up and changes in place. The pipeline a few slides on does both.

<!-- step -->

- The notes split the same way, so **N** shows what to say at this click.

<!-- step -->

> Printing gives one page per click, like a Beamer handout.
slides.notes:
Four clicks on this slide, and a part of the notes for each.
<!-- step -->
The marker is `<!-- step -->`: an HTML comment, so any other markdown renderer shows nothing.
<!-- step -->
In a figure that is `data-step="3"` for "there from click three" and `data-until="4"` for "gone at click four".
<!-- step -->
This is the part you are reading now: the projector shows it alone and keeps the others quieter.
<!-- step -->
The editor shows every step at once, because the whole slide is what you edit.
slides.summary: Steps in the text: what follows a marker waits for the next click.

slides.title: A chart is a drawing too
slides.body:
Figures are SVG: text a model can read, git can diff and you can edit. A chart is no exception.
This one is a few dozen lines, and its bars grow by CSS alone.

Ask for "a log scale" or "add the PDF" and it comes back as a change to those lines, not as a new picture.

> Small follows from legible: 237 slides in 1 MB.

<!-- col -->

![[fig-size-chart]]
slides.summary: Figures are SVG, charts included, which is why they can be edited and why the deck is small.

slides.title: Edit on the slide
slides.body:
![[fig-figure-editing]]

<!-- col -->

Click a title to change it. Hover a paragraph for a grip to drag it, a `＋` to insert below it.

Click a figure and its editor opens on the drawing: select a shape, move it, recolour it, join
two boxes with an arrow that re-routes itself when either moves.

> Every gesture is one `Ctrl-Z`.
slides.summary: You edit on the slide itself, at the size the room will see.

slides.title: A screenshot, with the drawing on top
slides.notes:
The picture is a screenshot of this editor. It is kept once in the deck, shrunk to what a projector shows, and described in words: a model is told the description, never the pixels, and may crop it or draw on it but never redraw it. The callouts are SVG on top, one per click.
<!-- step -->
The slide list, by section: drag to reorder, select several and Ctrl-C them into another deck, figures and all.
<!-- step -->
The slide itself, at the size the room sees: click and type.
<!-- step -->
Under the slide, the bar that inserts the next block: a heading, a list, a table, a formula, code, a figure, a click.
<!-- step -->
On the right, what the slide is for, its layout, and the AI: analyse, tighten, or say exactly what to change.
<!-- step -->
The menu is the deck: settings, theme, layouts, export. Present starts the show.
slides.summary: Pictures for what cannot be drawn, with SVG callouts on top that arrive click by click.

slides.title: Ask, and argue back
slides.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Say what a slide is for** | one line, and it writes the slide to serve it |
| **Ask for changes** | *cut the third bullet, the figure already says it* |
| **Analyse this slide** | it writes what it would change into a box you can edit |
| **Suggest what goes here** | three named moves, with the question each answers |

***

> Strike out what you disagree with. What is left is what runs.
slides.notes: Every AI action is a proposal you accept or discard, and one Ctrl-Z puts the slide back. The panels run on your own key under studio.sh, or on a small daily allowance in this demo.
slides.summary: How the AI is used in practice: a first draft and a critic, never the author.

slides.title: Hand your agent an old deck
slides.body:
![[fig-agent-pipeline]]

> Your agent follows `docs/CONVERT.md` and `AGENTS.md`: words as markdown, diagrams redrawn, pictures only where nothing else will do.
slides.notes:
Give Claude Code, or any coding agent, the link to the repository and the file.
<!-- step -->
ingest.py reads the deck without a model: every slide's text in reading order, its tables, the numbers behind its charts, its pictures and notes.
<!-- step -->
A diagram arrives as a picture of a diagram…
<!-- step -->
…and the agent redraws it as SVG, which you and it can edit afterwards. This is one figure: the bitmap leaves at the click the drawing arrives.
<!-- step -->
shots.mjs photographs every slide at every click, and the agent looks at the pictures before it says it is done.
<!-- step -->
Out comes one HTML file that presents from a link.
slides.summary: A coding agent converts a PowerPoint into a SlAIdy deck by itself; the figure builds up one stage a click.

slides.title: Present, rehearse, keep time
slides.body:
#### In the room

**P** presents, on the projector when one is plugged in; **D** moves it to the other display.

**N** shows the notes for this click, **O** every slide at once.

<!-- col -->

#### Rehearsing

**H** shows the hidden slides too. The next slide is one.

A note can start with the time the slide should be reached at.

<!-- col -->

#### On its own

`?auto=20` moves on every 20 seconds, at a PechaKucha's pace; **A** pauses.

[Watch this deck do it](https://kordikp.github.io/slaidy/?auto=5#present)
slides.summary: What the projector does, in three columns.

slides.title: For the speaker only
slides.body:
You see this slide because you pressed **H**, or because you are editing. In the room it is
skipped, and the slide list shows it struck through.

Keep the backup here: the answer to the question you expect, the slide you cut for time, the
teacher's key.
slides.summary: A hidden slide, shown only when rehearsing with H or editing.

slides.title: One deck, any look
slides.body:
![[fig-themes|94%]]

One slide of a lecture in eight themes. Pick one under **⋯ → Deck settings → Style → Theme**; the deck keeps
it inside, so it still opens offline. Bring yours as a [pull request](https://github.com/kordikp/slaidy/blob/main/themes/README.md).
slides.summary: Themes: the same slide in eight looks, and how to bring your own.

slides.title: Take it with you
slides.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **PDF** | the browser's own print engine, one page per click; nothing is uploaded |
| **Markdown** | the folder you started with: `slides/*.md` and `figures/*.svg` |
| **One HTML file** | the deck inside the editor: opens from a disk, presents from a link |
| **An article** | the whole deck as text with its figures, for Substack or a `.docx` |
| **The web** | `publish.py` makes a link that presents, and the notes as a page |
| **GitLab** | a deck published there saves straight back, as markdown, under your name |
slides.summary: The exits, because a format you cannot leave is a trap.
